nameStory: The "tomatillo" name comes from the Spanish word "tomatl," meaning tomato, with the diminutive "-illo" added - so it literally means "little tomato." Despite the name similarity, tomatillos are only distant cousins to true tomatoes, though both belong to the nightshade family. The "large-flowered" part of this species' name helps distinguish it from other groundcherries in the same genus.
description: Large-flowered tomatillo is a bushy annual plant that grows 2-4 feet tall and wide, originally from Mexico but sometimes found growing wild in New England gardens and waste areas. The plant produces small, round, green or purple-tinged fruits that are completely enclosed in a papery, lantern-like husk that looks like a tiny Chinese lantern. Each fruit is about the size of a cherry tomato and sits snugly inside its beige, veined wrapper. This is the same plant that produces tomatillos used in Mexican cooking, especially salsa verde.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round, green or greenish-purple fruits completely enclosed in a papery, lantern-shaped husk that feels dry and crinkly to the touch. The husk has prominent veins and splits open when the fruit is ripe.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Yellow, five-petaled flowers about 3/4 inch across with dark purple or brown spots at the base of each petal. Flowers have a slightly sweet, mild fragrance and bloom singly from leaf joints.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to egg-shaped leaves, 2-4 inches long, with slightly toothed edges and a soft, somewhat sticky texture. Leaves are arranged alternately on the stem and have a mild tomato-like scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy, sprawling plant that grows 2-4 feet tall and equally wide, with branching stems that may lean or sprawl as the plant matures and becomes heavy with fruit.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Green to purplish stems that feel slightly sticky or tacky to the touch, especially near the growing tips and flower clusters.

habitat: In New England, large-flowered tomatillo is typically found as an escape from cultivation in disturbed soils around gardens, compost piles, and waste areas. It prefers full sun and well-drained, fertile soil, often appearing in areas where garden waste has been dumped or where seeds have been scattered from kitchen scraps.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms. Young plants emerge with their characteristic sticky stems and soft, oval leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants bloom from mid to late summer with yellow flowers marked by dark spots. This is when the plant is most easily identified by its distinctive blossoms.
seasonality.fall: Fruits develop and ripen in their papery husks through late summer and early fall. The husks turn tan and become very dry and rustly.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die with first frost, leaving behind dried stems and sometimes persistent husks that rattle in the wind.

funFact: Tomatillos are actually more closely related to cape gooseberries than to tomatoes, and unlike tomatoes, they're self-incompatible - meaning you need at least two plants for fruit production because they can't pollinate themselves!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other groundcherries in the Physalis genus, but large-flowered tomatillo has the largest flowers and fruits of the group. Memory trick: if the fruit fills most of its papery husk and the flower is bigger than a dime, it's likely the large-flowered tomatillo rather than its smaller relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "large-flowered tomatillo," this is actually the common tomatillo of Mexican cuisine - the "large-flowered" designation is mainly used by botanists to distinguish it from other Physalis species. Many people don't realize that the tomatillos in grocery stores come from plants that can grow wild in New England.
compareHints: Large-flowered tomatillo differs from other New England groundcherries by having the largest flowers (3/4 inch across) and fruits that nearly fill their husks. Clammy groundcherry and hairy groundcherry have much smaller fruits that rattle loosely in their husks, while cape gooseberry has orange fruits and is rarely found growing wild in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's groundcherries, clammy groundcherry stands out for its distinctly sticky texture – other species like hairy groundcherry are fuzzy but not sticky, while strawberry groundcherry tends to be more smooth.
